hook.en: A Car, a Bus and a Bike all have a speed and a number plate. Write those once in a Vehicle class and let each one inherit them.

objectives.en: Use super to call the superclass constructor and members
Explain access specifiers and the types of inheritance Java supports

narration.en: A Car, a Bus and a Bike all have a speed and a number plate. Write those once in a Vehicle class and let each one inherit them.

body.en: Inheritance lets a new class (subclass, derived or child class) acquire the fields and methods of an existing class (superclass, base or parent class): class Car extends Vehicle { … }. It models an is-a relationship: a Car is a Vehicle. The subclass can add new members and redefine (override) inherited methods. Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance of classes, but not multiple inheritance of classes (one class cannot extend two classes); interfaces fill that gap.

title.en: On the board: a subclass with super

say.en: The subclass calls the superclass constructor with super(...), which must be its first statement.

text.en: Student(String n, int r) { super(n); roll = r; }

say.en: super.show() runs the parent version inside the overriding child version.

narration.en: Let us build up a subclass with super on the board, one step at a time.

prompt.en: class A { A() { print("A"); } } class B extends A { B() { print("B"); } } class C extends B { C() { print("C"); } }. Put the events of new C() in order.

narration.en: class A { A() { print("A"); } } class B extends A { B() { print("B"); } } class C extends B { C() { print("C"); } }. Put the events of new C() in order.

steps.en: C() first calls super(), that is B()
B() first calls super(), that is A()

explanation.en: Constructors run from the top of the hierarchy down: each first calls its superclass constructor (implicitly if super() is not written). The output is ABC.

body.en: Access specifiers control who can see a member. private: only inside its own class (not inherited in a visible way). default (no keyword): any class in the same package. protected: the same package and subclasses, even in other packages. public: everywhere. A subclass cannot reach the private members of its superclass directly; it uses public or protected methods (getters and setters) instead. This keeps data encapsulated while allowing reuse.

prompt.en: A member of class Person in package school. Can class Student extends Person in package exam access it?

narration.en: A member of class Person in package school. Can class Student extends Person in package exam access it?

explanation.en: Across packages a subclass sees public and protected members; default members are package-only and private members are class-only.

problem.en: Find the output: class P { int x = 10; void m() { System.out.print("P" + x + " "); } } class Q extends P { int x = 20; void m() { System.out.print("Q" + x + " "); super.m(); } } … new Q().m();

steps.en: Q's m runs: x inside Q is Q's own x = 20, so it prints Q20.
super.m() runs P's m, where x is P's x = 10: prints P10.

narration.en: Find the output: class P { int x = 10; void m() { System.out.print("P" + x + " "); } } class Q extends P { int x = 20; void m() { System.out.print("Q" + x + " "); super.m(); } } … new Q().m();

body.en: In a constructor, super(...) must be the very first statement. If you do not write it, Java quietly inserts super() with no arguments, which fails if the parent has no such constructor.
